references.text: The father's words are repeated almost verbatim in Luke 15:32, where the father explains to the older brother that "your brother was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found." This shows that the joy over the return of the lost one is the central message of the parable.

In the parable of the lost sheep in Luke 15:6-7, we find the same pattern: what was lost is found, and it is celebrated with joy. The joy over finding what was lost is a recurring theme throughout Luke 15.

In the parable of the lost coin in Luke 15:9-10, there is celebration when the coin is found, just as the father celebrates the return of his son. Joy in heaven over one sinner who repents is the parallel.

Paul describes in Ephesians 2:1-5 how believers were "dead in their trespasses and sins" but were made alive with Christ. The expression "νεκρὸς ἦν καὶ ἀνέζησεν" (was dead and is alive again) in the parable reflects this same spiritual transition from death to life.

In Romans 6:13, Paul urges believers to present themselves to God "as those who have been brought from death to life." This uses the same imagery of the transition from spiritual death to life as the father's description of the lost son.

John writes in 1 John 3:14 that "we know that we have passed out of death into life." The transition from death to life described in the parable of the lost son is mirrored in this theological truth about salvation and new life.

In Ezekiel's vision of the dry bones in Ezekiel 37:3, God asks whether the dead bones can live again. The prophecy of restoration from death to life is an Old Testament parallel to the theme "was dead and is alive again" in the parable.

In Revelation 3:1, Christ says to the church in Sardis: "You have the reputation of being alive, but you are dead." This contrasts with the lost son who was dead but came back to life, showing that spiritual death and life are a recurring biblical theme.

Paul writes in 2 Corinthians 5:17 that "if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation; the old has passed away, behold, the new has come." The return and celebration of the lost son illustrate this radical renewal from loss to restoration.
